description: Assess your depth in EVM architecture, Solidity syntax, reentrancy guards, ERC token standards, and gas efficiency.

questions.question: Which EVM memory area is persistent between function calls and writes directly to blockchain state?
options: Memory
Storage
Calldata
Stack
questions.explanation: Storage is the persistent key-value store associated with a smart contract on the EVM. Memory and Calldata are temporary.

questions.question: What is the primary vulnerability in a classic reentrancy attack?
options: Using tx.origin instead of msg.sender
Performing an external call before updating the internal contract balance state
Integer overflow when computing reward tokens
Missing visibility specifiers on contract variables
questions.explanation: Reentrancy occurs when an external call yields control to an attacker contract before internal balances or flags are updated (Checks-Effects-Interactions violation).

questions.question: In Solidity 0.8+, what happens automatically upon arithmetic overflow or underflow?
options: The number silently wraps around like standard C integers
The transaction automatically reverts with a Panic(0x11) error
The EVM sets an overflow flag that can only be cleared with SafeMath
The contract self-destructs to preserve state integrity
questions.explanation: Solidity 0.8.0 introduced default checked arithmetic. Any overflow or underflow will trigger an automatic revert unless wrapped inside an unchecked { ... } block.

questions.question: Which function visibility modifier allows a function to ONLY be called externally from outside the contract?
options: public
private
external
internal
questions.explanation: Functions marked 'external' can only be called from outside the contract or via 'this.functionName()' within the contract.

questions.question: Which ERC standard defines non-fungible tokens (NFTs) with unique token IDs?
options: ERC-20
ERC-721
questions.explanation: ERC-721 is the standard for Non-Fungible Tokens where every token ID represents a unique, non-interchangeable asset.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the 'indexed' keyword in Solidity event declarations?
options: It encrypts the log data so only miners can view it
It places topic hashes into the Bloom filter for rapid off-chain filtering
It ensures the event can be called like an internal function
It forces the event data to be stored permanently in contract storage
questions.explanation: Up to 3 parameters in an event can be marked 'indexed', allowing clients and indexers (like The Graph) to filter logs efficiently using topics.

questions.question: What is the key advantage of 'immutable' variables over 'constant' variables in Solidity?
options: Immutable variables can be reassigned multiple times during execution
Immutable variables can be assigned once dynamically inside the constructor at deploy time
Immutable variables consume zero deployment bytecode
Immutable variables are stored in contract storage rather than bytecode
questions.explanation: 'constant' must be fixed at compile time, whereas 'immutable' can be evaluated or assigned dynamically in the constructor and then permanently baked into bytecode.

questions.question: Which opcode is executed when ETH is sent to a contract without calldata, provided it is implemented?
options: fallback()
receive()
default()
payable()
questions.explanation: The 'receive() external payable' function is executed whenever a contract receives plain Ether with empty calldata. If absent, fallback() is called.

title: Web3 & Solidity Smart Contract Mastery

description: Evaluate your understanding of React 19 hooks, state synchronization, Web3 provider integration, and client-side performance.

questions.question: In Wagmi v2, which hook is primarily used to invoke state-changing smart contract functions?
options: useReadContract
useWriteContract
useContractCall
useSignTransaction
questions.explanation: useWriteContract (and writeContractAsync) is the standard Wagmi hook to broadcast state-modifying smart contract transactions.

questions.question: Why should you avoid mutating React state objects directly (e.g. state.count = 5)?
options: React state objects are frozen by the V8 JavaScript engine
React relies on reference equality to detect changes and trigger efficient re-renders
Direct mutation throws an uncatchable WebAssembly panic
It will cause automatic network requests to synchronize with local storage
questions.explanation: React compares object references (shallow comparison). Mutating an object keeps the same reference, causing React to miss the update and fail to re-render.

questions.question: What is the primary benefit of React.useMemo?
options: To persist data across browser tabs and sessions
To memoize expensive calculation results between component re-renders
To automatically handle async API error boundaries
To convert functional components into class components
questions.explanation: useMemo caches the result of a calculation between renders until one of its declared dependencies changes.

questions.question: What hook would you use to synchronize component lifecycle with an external wallet provider like window.ethereum?
options: useRef
useEffect
useTransition
useId
questions.explanation: useEffect is designed to manage side effects, such as subscribing to wallet provider events ('accountsChanged', 'chainChanged').

questions.question: In React, what is the role of the unique 'key' prop when rendering lists?
options: It sets the HTML element id attribute in the DOM
It helps React identify which items have changed, been added, or been removed during reconciliation
It provides CSS scoping for nested styles
It encrypts the list item data for secure transmission
questions.explanation: Keys give elements a stable identity across renders so React can reorder, insert, or remove DOM nodes efficiently without unnecessary re-creation.

questions.question: When using wagmi's useAccount hook, what property returns the currently connected user's Ethereum address?
options: userAddress
account
address
currentWallet
questions.explanation: useAccount() returns an object containing 'address', 'isConnected', 'status', and connector details.

title: Frontend Engineering with Modern React & Wagmi

description: Test your mastery over Automated Market Makers (AMM), constant product formulas, impermanent loss, and flash loans.

questions.question: What is the foundational invariant formula utilized by Uniswap V2 AMM pools?
options: x + y = k
x * y = k
x / y = k
questions.explanation: Uniswap V2 uses the Constant Product Market Maker formula: x * y = k, where x and y represent the reserves of the two pooled tokens.

questions.question: What is 'Impermanent Loss' in the context of automated liquidity provision?
options: The loss suffered when a private key is lost during bridging
The difference in portfolio value between holding tokens in an AMM pool versus holding them in a wallet when prices diverge
The gas fee spent when transactions fail due to slippage
The penalty assessed by validator nodes during slashing events
questions.explanation: Impermanent loss measures the opportunity cost of providing liquidity compared to simply holding the tokens when the external price ratio shifts.

questions.question: What unique property makes Flash Loans possible in DeFi?
options: Zero collateral is required as long as the borrowed funds plus fee are returned within the exact same atomic transaction
They can only be executed by centralized banks registered on Ethereum
They grant flash governance voting power that persists for 24 hours
They bypass Ethereum gas fees by routing through sidechains
questions.explanation: Flash loans allow uncollateralized borrowing because the EVM is atomic: if the loan is not fully repaid with fee by the end of the transaction execution, the entire transaction reverts.

questions.question: What does an Oracle (such as Chainlink) primarily provide to DeFi protocols?
options: Cold storage backup for protocol treasury funds
Cryptographically verified off-chain real-world data (such as asset price feeds)
Automatic smart contract deployment across Layer 2 rollups
Zero-knowledge proving algorithms for Ethereum consensus
questions.explanation: Oracles bridge off-chain data (such as crypto/fiat price feeds, weather, sports) onto blockchains so smart contracts can execute deterministically.

questions.question: What is 'Slippage' during a decentralized exchange swap?
options: The latency caused by slow internet connection
The difference between the expected price of a trade and the actual execution price due to pool depth and price impact
The commission retained by the front-end interface
The gas fee adjustment made by MetaMask EIP-1559
questions.explanation: Slippage occurs when trades move the price along the constant product curve or when other transactions execute before yours in the mempool.

title: DeFi Architecture & Protocol Economics

description: Assess your capability in detecting critical security vulnerabilities including access control flaws, flash loan attacks, and front-running.

questions.question: Why is relying on 'tx.origin' for authorization in smart contracts dangerous?
options: tx.origin is deprecated and will be removed in next hard fork
It makes the contract susceptible to phishing attacks where an authorized user is tricked into calling a malicious contract
tx.origin always returns the zero address on layer 2 networks
tx.origin cannot sign multi-sig transactions
questions.explanation: If an authorized contract owner calls an attacker's malicious contract, the attacker's contract can call the protected function and tx.origin will still equal the owner's address.

questions.question: What is a Front-Running attack (or Sandwich Attack) in a decentralized mempool?
options: An attacker steals the private key while the user is typing
An attacker monitors pending transactions in the mempool and pays higher gas fees to get their transaction mined before the victim's trade
A brute force attack against elliptic curve scalar multiplication
A DDoS attack against Ethereum RPC endpoints
questions.explanation: In transparent public mempools, bots can observe pending trades and submit transactions with higher gas prices to front-run or sandwich the victim.

questions.question: What does the 'Checks-Effects-Interactions' pattern prevent?
options: Flash loan liquidity drain
Reentrancy attacks
Block timestamp manipulation
Gas limit exhaustion
questions.explanation: Checking conditions first, updating internal state second, and only then interacting with external contracts prevents reentrant callers from exploiting stale states.

questions.question: Which tool is widely used for static analysis of Solidity code to discover known vulnerabilities?
options: Slither
Webpack
TailwindCSS
Postman
questions.explanation: Slither is a leading open-source static analysis framework for Solidity developed by Trail of Bits.

questions.question: Why should 'block.timestamp' NOT be used as a source of secure randomness?
options: It is measured in nanoseconds which causes arithmetic overflow
Miners/validators have minor leeway to manipulate timestamps within a tolerable window to influence random outcomes in their favor
The EVM does not have access to timestamps
It is static for all blocks on the blockchain
questions.explanation: Validators can tweak block timestamps by several seconds to bias outcomes in lotteries or random mints. Chainlink VRF or commit-reveal schemes should be used instead.
